title: The snake that was told not to bite
hookLine: a snake promises not to bite, and the village boys find out
carry: ahimsa: never bite, but you may hiss
tomorrow: The salt doll and the ocean

lines: A SNAKE BY THE VILLAGE PATH.
cards: A village path has a problem: a snake lives beside it, and it bites. People take the long way around. Then a holy man comes walking down that path, unafraid, and the snake rises to strike.
He calms it with a few words and gives it a teaching. Ramakrishna told this story in his room at Dakshineswar to visitors who lived ordinary lives, with jobs, families and difficult neighbors.
It's a funny story, with a serious point.

teach.b: The holy man gives the snake a sacred name to repeat and tells it: stop biting. Harm no one.
That's ahimsa, non-harm, the first of the yamas that open the Yoga Sutras' eight limbs, and one of the oldest ideals in Hinduism. The snake takes it to heart, and stops.
Soon the cowherd boys of the village notice the dangerous snake is harmless now. They throw stones at it. They grab it by the tail, whirl it around and dash it on the ground.
The snake drags itself, half dead, into its hole, and grows thin, barely eating. Later the holy man comes back and finds his disciple, bruised and thin. What happened to you?
You told me not to bite, the snake says. So I didn't. And look at me.
The holy man answers: I told you not to bite.

teach.h: I NEVER TOLD YOU NOT TO HISS.
teach.b: I never told you not to hiss. Ramakrishna draws it out for the people in the room. Someone living in the world, he says, should harm no one.

But they may need to raise a hiss, so that others don't take advantage. Many teachers read this as a line drawn inside ahimsa itself. Non-harm is about what you do to others: no bite, no venom, no wish to wound.
It was never a vow to let yourself, or the people in your care, be destroyed.
He gives this parable to householders, people with offices, families and neighbors who push, whose dharma includes protecting what's been put in their hands.

teach.h: A HISS IS NOT A BITE.

how: Ramakrishna's parables, like the snake that was told not to bite, are retold in talks and study circles at Ramakrishna Math and Mission centers, often as practical guidance for people living family lives.

games.q: you're the snake. you promised not to bite, and now the village boys are throwing stones at you. what does the holy man say you should have done?
o: bitten them; the promise doesn't count anymore.
games.why: I told you not to bite; I never told you not to hiss. Ramakrishna's point for householders: keep ahimsa, harm no one, but non-harm was never a vow to be destroyed.

practice: Bring to mind one place where you've been walked on: at work, at home, online. First, ahimsa: let go of any wish to hurt that person back.
If you pray, repeat a name of God, the way the holy man gave the snake a sacred name, then say this person's name and ask for their good.

Then, the hiss: calmly find one clear sentence you could say there, true and firm, without wanting to wound, and hold it gently, like something you may need later. If you don't pray, simply wish them well in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Ramakrishna. The mystic of Dakshineswar who could talk of God in one breath and, in the next, tell a snake it was allowed to hiss.
